newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Mining community wary over Indonesian gold row.
newsitem.headline: Mining community wary over Indonesian gold row.

text.p: The international mining community is watching the turmoil over one of world's largest gold finds with apprehension, fearing it could make doing business in Indonesia more complicated.

The issue centres on the small Canadian mining firm Bre-X Minerals Ltd and its stake in the Busang area, which it estimates holds at least 57 million ounces of gold in Indonesia's East Kalimantan province.

Bre-X is seeking a partner to provide the funds needed to develop the site amid jungle-fringed papaya plantations on Borneo island. The costs and potential profits are huge -- the current value of the gold amounts to more than $21 billion.

The government is pressing Bre-X to link up with one of the world's biggest gold miners, Barrick Gold Corp, and is seeking 10 percent of the action. Two members of President Suharto's family are also involved in the long-running saga.
Some mining executives and analysts hope the battle of Busang is a one-off affair, and will not influence Indonesian mining policy, which so far has had a good reputation on the international scene.
"It's an anomaly, a one-off, rather than the average," said Laurie Fitzgerald, an analyst for Perth-based stock broker Hartley-Poynton Ltd.

A senior mining executive, who asked not to be named, said: "The situation is so delicate at the moment, one is best leaving the Indonesian government and the individuals to arrange this affair as they see fit."

Indonesian mining officials have said Bre-X and Barrick have responded "positively" to a government proposal that Barrick takes 75 percent of the find and Bre-X 25 percent. The smaller company insists no deal has yet been reached.
One mining source said it was unprecedented for the government to recommend a partner: "It is wrong. In my 30 years in the mining sector, I have not seen anything like this."
Until there is an agreement, the government is withholding the necessary contracts of work needed to continue exploration and development of the property.

There is also alarm at the involvement of two of President Suharto's children. Bre-X said it had signed up a company headed by his eldest son Sigit Harjojudanto, offering $40 million over 40 months and a 10-percent stake in Busang's richest part.
Barrick, which has such figures as former U.S. president George Bush and former Canadian prime minster Brian Mulroney on its board, has raised some eyebrows through its activities.
It has teamed up with a firm run by Suharto's eldest daughter, Siti Hardianti Rukmana, in what Barrick described as a partnership "to prepare for a potential mining development project".
Diplomatic sources said Suharto himself was concerned over the high-profile involvement of family members in the issue.
Tarnishing the glitter further is a potential law suit by Indonesian businessman Yusuf Merukh, who claims 40 percent of Busang.
A senior international mining source said Indonesia "had got a very good reputation so far, not reneging on the deals they've come up with over the years".

"The contract of work has been pretty sacrosanct, they've always stuck by it. Now this could be construed in the mining community that if you spend a lot of money investigating and drilling and so forth, they're not to be trusted any more."
If the deal between Bre-X and Barrick falls through, other major companies have shown interest in the deposit. These include Place Dome Inc, Newmont Mining Corp and Teck Corp.

Bre-X and Barrick are both listed on the Toronto Stock Exchange and the latter in New York also. So in addition to the other problems there are regulatory hurdles to be overcome to satisfy the exchanges and company shareholders.
